at.topic: ISA-95 hierarchy and the automation pyramid
at.quote: enterprise → site → area → line/cell → equipment → sensor

items.item: The Purdue Reference Model is a five-level hierarchy from the physical process (Level 0) up through controllers, operator stations, plant operations, enterprise systems, and a corporate level added later

at.step: Five levels, one vocabulary for everything that follows

items.item: The iDMZ sits at Level 3.5, its own zone not part of OT or IT; no traffic crosses the boundary without terminating in the iDMZ first, and OT systems should never initiate connections toward the enterprise network

at.step: A zone of its own, and a guarantee that is physical, not configured

items.item: An MQTT broker in the iDMZ receives Sparkplug B publications from the OT zone and exposes topic subscriptions to IT-side consumers, acting as the single controlled egress point

at.step: Stall the consumer, then watch what the OT source actually feels

sources.source: Network Critical: Data Diodes for IEC 62443

items.item: A data diode uses separate physical transmit and receive paths to physically enforce one-way data flow; reverse traffic is not possible regardless of configuration, unlike a firewall's software rules

at.step: A zone of its own, and a guarantee that is physical, not configured

items.item: OPC UA is a platform-independent standard for secure, reliable communication between diverse industrial systems and devices, with its own security model covering authentication, encryption and integrity

items.item: Sparkplug defines an MQTT topic namespace, payload and session-state management for real-time SCADA/control HMI requirements; its birth and death certificates let a subscriber know what exists and whether it is connected without polling

sources.source: HiveMQ: Smart Manufacturing Using ISA95, MQTT Sparkplug and the UNS

items.item: A unified namespace lets participants publish to a central repository instead of contacting each other directly; ISA-95 is a functional modeling standard, not a networking one, and is complementary to a unified namespace architecture

items.item: The hook's point is that the direct connection itself is the architectural risk, not that the analytics query was poorly written; a learner who answers 'optimize the query' has missed the point the predict step exists to correct

at.step: A dashboard connects straight to SCADA, for simplicity

items.item: The predict step's correct answer names the specific architectural fix (a buffer between source and consumer) rather than a performance fix (a faster or less frequent query); a learner who picks either performance option has only lowered the odds of the same failure, not removed it

at.step: Before the levels: what actually has to change here?

items.item: The Purdue-levels step states the five-level hierarchy precisely as Process Control Guide's own definitions, including that Level 5 was added later rather than being original to the model; a learner should place a named system on its level, not just recite the list

at.step: Five levels, one vocabulary for everything that follows

items.item: The diode step's point is that the one-way guarantee is physical (separate transmit/receive paths), not merely 'more secure' in a vague sense; a learner should be able to state why a diode survives a misconfiguration that would defeat a firewall rule

at.step: A zone of its own, and a guarantee that is physical, not configured

items.item: The three-mechanisms step is careful to state what each mechanism answers that the others don't (direct read vs. existence/connectivity vs. historical record), not a ranking of which mechanism is simply 'best'

at.step: Three ways to read from the plant floor, each for something different

items.item: The buffer-isolation step's proof is run both ways (unbuffered propagates the stall, buffered does not) in examples.py, not asserted only in prose; a learner should understand this as a provable property, not a design intention

at.step: Stall the consumer, then watch what the OT source actually feels

items.item: The unified-namespace step is explicit that ISA-95 and a UNS solve different problems (how systems talk vs. what the data means) rather than presenting them as competing or interchangeable standards, sourced from HiveMQ's own framing

at.step: One namespace every system publishes to, instead of wiring each pair by hand

items.item: The final predict step's correct answer identifies the missing edge buffer as the failure, not a Purdue-level violation or a missing diode; MES reading a PLC directly is architecturally normal, so a learner who flags the levels or recommends a diode has missed that the actual gap is the lack of any buffer at all

at.step: Prove it

items.item: This topic cannot connect to a real PLC, SCADA system or MQTT broker in this sandbox; examples.py reproduces Purdue-level classification and the backpressure-isolation proof as a disclosed structural simulation against synthetic events, not a live deployment
